notes:
I've written notes for every verse below. A few limits first, since I ran out of searches and page fetches before I could check everything:

- **Missing sources:** I didn't reach netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, catholic.com, oca.org, any Lutheran site, or Ellicott's and Gill's full comments. Those views are left out.
- **Prosperity, word of faith and hyper-grace:** I found nothing on these for this psalm, so there are no notes on them.
- **Denominational disagreements:** The sources I read mostly agree. The one real disagreement I found is over verse 11, and it's a translation question between individual teachers, not a stated position of any church. For context on who's who: Calvin is Reformed, Spurgeon is Baptist, Adam Clarke is Methodist, Matthew Henry is Presbyterian/Nonconformist, and David Guzik (enduringword) is on your Pentecostal/charismatic list.
- **Augustine:** He is the only Catholic source I read. I used the parts of his Exposition of Psalm 7 on newadvent.org that came up in search results (comments up to v. 10).
- **Pulpit Commentary:** I read its whole Psalm 7 page (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/7.htm). That page had no sentence markers I could cite, so where I use it I give the link without a citation tag.

---

**Title / v. 1**
- **"Shiggaion":** Its meaning is uncertain. It appears only here and in Habakkuk 3:1, and its meaning is unknown. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/7.htm
  - Spurgeon reads it as "variable songs," with which also the idea of solace and pleasure is associated. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps007.php
  - Clarke derives it from shagah, to wander, a wandering song; i.e., a Psalm composed by David in his wanderings while hiding from Saul. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/psalms/7.htm
  - BSB's own note: Shiggaion is probably a musical or liturgical term. https://biblehub.com/psalms/7.htm
- **Who was Cush?** Three views:
  - **Code name for Saul.** Clarke calls it probably a name of disguise for Saul, the son of Kish. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/psalms/7.htm. The Pulpit Commentary leans toward the view of Hengstenberg, that Saul is meant. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-7.html
  - **One of Saul's men.** Matthew Henry thinks it more likely some kinsman of Saul named Cush who painted David as a traitor. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_007.cfm. Guzik agrees: simply another partisan of Saul against David. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-7/
  - **Shimei.** Guzik also mentions this possibility (2 Samuel 16:5). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-7/
- **"Take refuge":** The Hebrew word means "to flee;" to flee to a place; to take shelter (Barnes). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/7-1.htm
- **The theme:** Spurgeon calls the psalm the SONG OF THE SLANDERED SAINT. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps007.php
- **"My God":** Calvin says calling God "my God" works as a bulwark that beats back the waves of temptations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/7.htm

**v. 2**
- **Plural to singular:** The Pulpit Commentary notes the switch from many pursuers to one, and thinks the one enemy David fears is probably Saul. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/7.htm
- **The lion:** Guzik quotes Maclaren that the image suits a shepherd king, who had taken a lion by the beard. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-7/
- **Slander wounds:** Spurgeon says the wounds of the tongue cut deeper than the flesh. He also applies the lion to the devil, who goes about like a lion, seeking whom he may devour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/7-1.htm
- **Catholic reading:** Augustine also takes the lion as the devil, quoting 1 Peter 5:8. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801007.htm

**vv. 3–4**
- **Not a claim to be sinless:** Teachers agree David isn't claiming perfection. He is denying the specific charge.
  - Guzik: David did not claim sinless perfection. Instead, he simply rejected the idea of moral equivalence between himself and his enemies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-7/
  - The Pulpit Commentary links the charge to the accusation that David "sought the king's hurt" (1 Samuel 24:9). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/7.htm
- **v. 4 can be translated two ways.** The Pulpit Commentary sets out both. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/7.htm
  - (a) KJV/RV: a side-comment, "yea, I have delivered him that without cause is mine enemy." This would point to David sparing Saul (1 Samuel 24 and 26).
  - (b) Hengstenberg and others: "if I have oppressed him who without cause is mine enemy." On this reading David denies wronging either friend or foe. The BSB follows a reading of this kind.
- **Calvin** takes the first sense: David had not only restrained himself from all revenge, but had even succoured his enemies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/7.htm
- **Catholic reading (Augustine):** He reads the verse as following Christ's patience, which he links to his reading of the title. Not repaying evil to someone you once helped shows an instance of greater patience. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801007.htm

**v. 5**
- **David's self-curse:** The Pulpit Commentary compares it to Job's self-curses (Job 31). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/7.htm
- Spurgeon: He had need have a golden character who dares to challenge such an ordeal. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps007.cfm
- **Catholic reading:** Augustine says the verse describes what really happens to those who repay evil. It is not what, as by an oath, he would imprecate on himself. He takes the singular "enemy" as the devil, the lion again. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801007.htm

**v. 6**
- **"Arise":** The Pulpit Commentary says this asks God to stop staying neutral and step in openly. It reads the last line as "judgment is a thing which thou hast ordained," so surely now is the time for it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/7.htm
- **God's anger:** Guzik warns against two errors. God is not without passions, but it is also a mistake to assume that the passions of God are always with us or support our opinion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-7/
- **Praying God's will:** Calvin, quoted by Spurgeon, teaches that we should in everything conform our requests to the divine will. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps007.php

**v. 7**
- **A worldwide courtroom:** The Cambridge Bible calls it The judgement scene. The Psalmist prays that 'the peoples' may be summoned to stand round the tribunal. No distinction is made between Israel and other nations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/7-7.htm
- **"Return on high":** This line is hard. The Pulpit Commentary reads it as God returning to his heavenly throne after judging. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/7-7.htm. The Expositor's Bible suggests a small change to the Hebrew text that gives "Sit Thou above it". The BSB's "take Your seat" is close to this. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/7.htm
- **The church:** The Geneva Bible notes: Not only for mine, but for your Church's sake declare your power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/7-7.htm
- **Catholic reading (Augustine):** He reads the verse about Christ. Those who crucified him did not understand him, and the Gentiles shall believe in You, and so shall the congregation of the people surround You. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801007.htm

**v. 8**
- **How can David appeal to his own righteousness?** The Reformed, Puritan and Calvary Chapel teachers I read all give the same answer: his righteousness is compared with his enemies', not perfection before God.
  - Calvin: David is comparing himself with his enemies, not answering for his whole life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/7.htm
  - Guzik: David looked for justice on the earthly level, justice between him and his false accuser. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-7/
  - Matthew Henry adds a gospel condition. Such an appeal comes after a man has made peace with God about all his sins, upon the terms of grace and mercy, through the sacrifice of the Mediator. He also says Christ alone could call on Heaven to attest his uprightness in all things. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/7-1.htm
- **Catholic reading (Augustine):** He contrasts this psalm with Psalm 6. There the sick person asks for healing by mercy. Here a person already made whole asks to be kept from falling back: Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801007.htm

**v. 9**
- **End the evil, not the people:** The Pulpit Commentary says David prays for the end of the wicked's wickedness, not of the wicked themselves. It explains "heart" as the seat of understanding and will, and "reins" (KJV for "minds") as natural impulses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/7.htm
- **Praying for the good too:** Matthew Henry: As we pray that the bad maybe made good, so we pray that the good may be made better. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_007.cfm
- **Catholic reading:** Augustine takes "reins" as a person's delights. Only God knows with what mind they are done. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801007.htm

**v. 10**
- **"My shield":** Literally "my shield is on God," meaning it is held up by him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/7.htm
- Matthew Henry: The upright in heart are safe, and ought to think themselves so, under the divine protection. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_007.cfm

**v. 11 (the one verse where readings really differ)**
- **The traditional reading:** God's anger continues against the wicked as long as their wickedness does. The Pulpit Commentary: There is no need of inserting the words, "with the wicked"… God's anger continues against the wicked as long as their wickedness continues. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/7.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** He asks how God can judge "every day" when he often delays punishment. His answer: no day passes without God showing that he tells the righteous from the wicked, so he never ceases to execute the office of a judge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/7.htm
- **Adam Clarke (Methodist):** He argues the better reading is "He is NOT angry every day." He blames the Chaldee (Aramaic) version for adding "with the wicked". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-7/
- **The Latin and Greek versions:** One of the "Explanatory Notes" collected in Spurgeon's Treasury of David says that, as the Vulgate and Septuagint suggest, the text points to a God whose anger does not burst forth in vengeance every day. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps007.cfm
- **Guzik:** He takes the traditional reading but adds that God's delay is not indifference but undeserved mercy giving sinners time to repent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-7/

**v. 12**
- **"He" is God:** The Pulpit Commentary takes the one who sharpens the sword to be God. It quotes Bishop Horne: he (i.e. God) will whet his sword. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/7.htm
- **God's patience:** Matthew Henry says that while God prepares, he gives the sinners timely warning of their danger, and space to repent. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_007.cfm
- **Readiness to judge:** Guzik: the sinner should never presume that God will delay His judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-7/

**v. 13**
- **Fiery arrows:** Hengstenberg, cited in the Pulpit Commentary, says that in sieges arrows were wrapped in burning material. It compares the "fiery darts" of Ephesians 6:16. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/7.htm
- **A strong warning:** Notes in Spurgeon's Treasury say no earlier psalm has had so frightful a threatening and indignation against the ungodly. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps007.php

**v. 14**
- **Pregnancy picture:** The "falsehood" born here is probably the false charges against David from vv. 3–5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/7.htm

**vv. 15–16**
- **The pit and the boomerang:** Both verses show the same rule of God's providence. Haman is the clearest example in Scripture. The Pulpit Commentary prefers to read v. 16 as a general statement rather than as dirt falling back into the pit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/7.htm
- **God's way of justice:** Guzik calls this God's righteous method of justice, where the calamity the wicked plan often returns upon their own head. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-7/
- **Catholic reading:** Augustine (in the Expositions edition hosted on monergism.com) cites these verses to show that when God punishes, he does not inflict His evil on them, but leaves them to their own evil. https://www.monergism.com/thethreshold/sdg/augustine/Expositions%20on%20the%20Book%20of%20Psal%20-%20Augustine.pdf

**v. 17**
- **Praise in advance:** The Pulpit Commentary says David thanks God for a deliverance he foresees and treats as already done. "The name of the LORD" stands for God himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/7.htm
- **"His righteousness":** Calvin says this means God's faithfulness which he makes good to his servants in defending and preserving their lives. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/7.htm
- Spurgeon: The slandered one is now a singer. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps007.php
- **Application:** Guzik says to praise God according to His righteousness rather than our own. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-7/
